Air Jordan fails to soar

Bullets and Jeff Malone hold Chicago's magnificent flyer to mere 25 in 106-103 victory

By Ken Murray

Evening Sun Staff

LANDOVER - Air Jordan descended on the Capital Centre with flames lapping at the engine and smoke billowing from the fuselage. The Chicago Bulls crashed and burned last night in a 106-103 loss to the Washington Bullets, but only after a crowd of 16,515 learned that Michael Jordan was mortal, after all. Mortality, in his case, is 25 points, five assists and three turnovers on a night when 29 points - five under his season average - would have won. And this is the price Jordan pays for being the most electrifying star in the NBA: He sits in front of his locker with long face and somber explanation for a performance that 95 percent of the players in the league would love to call their own. "I think we have to do it as a team," he said, dressed in brown leather from shoulders to shoes.

"One person can't do it." They can't? That grim assessment will come as hard news on the shores of Lake Michigan, where expectations for Jordan only begin with water-walking. Heaven knows Jordan tried last night. He struggled for three quarters, scoring only 13 points. In the fourth quarter, he strapped the Bulls to his back and sped down the runway. He was stopped just short of takeoff.

In the final 8:30 of the game, Jordan brought the Cap Centre crowd to its feet twice with dunks - this for a visiting player, remember - and scored 12 of the Bulls' 17 points. Four times, he gave the Bulls the lead. "When Michael tried to take over [in the fourth quarter], he did," said Wes Unseld, coach of the Bullets. It was too little, too late. Jordan's 30-foot jumper for the tying three points clanked off the front of the rim at the buzzer, and afterward the Bullets were thanking their local air-traffic controller.

"We didn't double-team Michael all the time, but that's what we intended to do to try to control him," Unseld said. "Jeff did a great job against him tonight." Give the latest round of their mano-a-mano to Bullets guard Jeff Malone, who outscored Jordan, 28-25, and had two fewer turnovers. There was a method to the madness, according to Jordan. "He comes out shooting the ball," Jordan said. "He comes straight at me, and their offense tries to make me work on defense.

Sometimes we should do the same thing and make him work. "They really concentrate on not letting me hurt them. That's one of the best team defenses I've played against." There is something about Jordan that brings out the best in Malone, who has fashioned some of his best games against the Bulls. "His jumping ability is unbelievable," Malone said. "He has those big hands like Doc [Julius Erving] and incredible hang time.

The good position to have him i in is in the air looking around for the basket."

When Unseld watches Jordan at work, he has flashbacks of another brilliant guard who inspired awe and amazement. "I always enjoy watching a guy do what I can't do," Unseld said. "It's like when I played with Earl Monroe. You find yourself standing around wondering how he did that. You find yourself doing the same thing with Michael." There were two such moments against the Bullets, and both came in the heat of the fourth quarter.

With 8:04 left, Jordan one-handed a missed bank shot by Scottie Pippen and in the same motion slam-dunked the ball for an 88-85 Chicago 1 lead. That shot immediately brought Malone off the bench, where he had been resting for the stretch run. The other memorable flight of fancy came with 1:24 to play. Bullets lose opener, 111-98, to Chicago

By Sam Davis

Sun Staff Correspondent

LANDOVER - Opening day for the Washington Bullets went about as expected. The Bullets were scrappy and aggressive on defense and they ran more on offense. They played with the Chicago Bulls and Michael Jordan for three quarters, but in the end, the lack of a dominant scorer and a rebounder sent the Bullets reeling to a 111-98 loss. With 5:12 left, the Bullets trailing, 102-88, and Jordan and the Bulls clearly in control, much of the crowd of 17,235 began heading for the exits.

Chicago was clinging to just a 81-77 advantage after three periods. But the Bullets ran out of gas early in the fourth quarter, as Chicago ran off 14 of the first 20 points, taking a 95-83 lead on John Paxson's threepoint field goal with 7:16 left. The Bullets never cut the lead to single digits the rest of the way. Jordan led the Bulls with 29 points but only a few were of the spectacular fashion the fans have come to expect from last year's most valuable player. It was second-year forward Horace Grant who hurt the Bullets the most.

With his younger brother Harvey looking on from the Bullets bench, Horace scored 25 points and grabbed 15, rebounds, leading the Bulls to a 50-37 rebounding advantage. There were some positive signs for the Bullets. Bernard King played well scoring a quiet 21 points, and rookie Ledell Eackles proved he may be capable of supplying the scoring punch the Bullets need. Eackles had 18 points. He hit from the perimeter and also showed some creative moves driving inside.

Free-agent center Dave Feitl was not impressive. He had one field-goal attempt, a lazy hook that did not touch the basket in the first half. He went to the bench not long after that shot and did not return. The Bullets trailed at the half, 54-51. They led, 51-50.

on a short jumper by King, but consecutive baskets by Horace Grant gave Chicago its four-point cushion. Chicago led by as much as seven in the first half. With their team ahead, 41-38, Jordan and Anthony Jones hit back-to-back jumpers to make it 45-38. The Bullets rallied to within 45-43 on a three-point play by King and a layup by Jeff Malone. The Bullets' largest first-half lead was 25-22 when Eackles hit a jumper off an assist from Dominic Pressley with 59 seconds left in the first quarter.

The Bullets did not lead by more than one the rest of the half. The Bullets' first-half performance was typical of what coach Wes Unseld sought. The Bullets were scrappy on defense and passed the ball well on offense. Chicago turned the ball over 12 times in the first half, and several of those turnovers were caused by the Bullets' defense. The Bullets had assists on all but one of their 22 first-half field goals.

Chicago wanted to exploit the Bullets inside where 6-foot-9 Charles Jones started at center. The Bulls tried to force the ball inside to Bill Cartwright, but Jones and the Bullets' defense kept Cartwright from dominating. Cartwright was just 1-for-5 from the floor. Still, the Bullets were hurt on the boards. Chicago out-rebounded the Bullets, 24-15, in the first half.

Horace Grant led the Bulls in scoring and rebounding with 12 points and nine rebounds. Jordan had 11 points in the first half and four assists, all in the opening period. King led the Bullets with 15 firsthalf points. He connected on six of eight field goals. Malone had nine points, but was off to a slow start from the floor, hitting just four of 11 shots.

The Bullets started slowly in the third quarter, hitting just two of their first eight s shots. Chicago ran off the six of the first eight points of the quarter to open its largest lead at 65-55. Eackles led the Bullets back with three straight baskets to trim the Chicago lead to 65-61. The Bullets drew even at 77-77 on a follow layup by John Williams, but Chicago scored the final four points of the quarter on a follow tap by Horace Grant and jumper from the top of the key by Dave Corzine, to take a 81-77 lead after three quarters. After turning the ball over just seven times in the first half, the Bullets had six third-quarter turnovers.

The Bullets played nearly all of the third period without Charles Jones, who was hit in the eye fighting for a rebound just after the half started. He went to the bench and sat with an ice pack over his left eye for the remainder of the quarter but started the fourth period.

56730613.title: File:United Center, Michael Jordan Statue, Chicago, Illinois (2519933299).jpg

ImageDescription.value:
The United Center is an indoor sports arena located in Chicago, Illinois. The United Center is home to both the Chicago Bulls of the National Basketball Association (NBA) and the Chicago Blackhawks of the National Hockey League (NHL). The arena is named after its corporate sponsor, United Airlines.

The plan to build the arena was created by Blackhawks owner Bill Wirtz and Bulls owner Jerry Reinsdorf. The United Center's predecessor was the indoor Chicago Stadium, the original "Madhouse on Madison", which was demolished after the newer arena opened for business on August 18, 1994. Due to the 1994–95 NHL lockout, the Blackhawks did not move in until January, 1995.

The east side of the stadium features statues of Michael Jordan (known as "The Spirit"), Bobby Hull and Stan Mikita, while a statue of various Blackhawks sits to the north on Madison Street, where the Chicago Stadium was located.
